articles.title: Arsenal transfer news: Gunners had more than 20 players on summer shortlist
articles.text:
Going into the summer transfer window as Premier League champions, hope sprang eternal for Arsenal.

An opportunity to capitalise, encouraged by a sense at Emirates Stadium that their competitors were in transition because of managerial instability.

If ever there was a moment to strike in recruitment, this was it.

The plans were ambitious: a shortlist with more than 20 players on it. They were targets at Real Madrid and Atletico Madrid, even at Chelsea and Tottenham.

But as the window shut on Tuesday night, you could not escape the sense of unfulfillment - certainly from a section of supporters.

Arsenal's close season was one characterised by some unquestionable successes, but also riddled by difficulties and frustration.

Ahead of their home match against Chelsea on Sunday, BBC Sport details Arsenal's transfer window and whether manager Mikel Arteta, sporting director Andrea Berta and, perhaps most pertinently, owners Kroenke Sports Entertainment can deem their summer operation a success.

Bruno Guimaraes's £75m capture from Newcastle United was Arsenal's most eye-catching signing.

Heading into the summer, Arsenal were keeping abreast of Guimaraes' situation at Newcastle, although others were considered a higher priority.

For instance, their interest in Elliot Anderson was widely reported, but it was clear the England international was joining Manchester City.

Guimaraes' former Newcastle team-mate Sandro Tonali and Bournemouth's Alex Scott were also among the midfielders explored before a move for the South American accelerated.

At the ages of 26 and 23 respectively, Tonali and Scott are younger than Guimaraes, who turns 29 in November.

But numerous factors, including availability and price - Tonali joined Spurs for a minimum £92m - made their signings difficult.

Aston Villa's Amadou Onana was also among the options considered, but the Belgium international suffered a serious knee injury at the World Cup.

By mid-June Guimaraes, who had universal backing inside the Emirates, emerged as the club's primary focus.

Berta knew the player's camp well and Guimaraes was admired by Arteta, who had made it clear he wanted proven talent to take his starting XI - rather than the wider squad - to greater heights.

Berta used his strong relationship with Guimaraes' representatives to facilitate Arsenal's move, hence why Newcastle maintained they had had no direct contact from the London club until days before his move was completed.

It is not uncommon for Berta to lean on intermediaries to conduct negotiations, although the approach has had varying degrees of success.

For instance, Arsenal actively sought moves for Leicester City teenagers Jeremy Monga and Louis Page over the summer.

But sources insist that the lack of club-to-club discussions meant both players ultimately did not join Arsenal, with Monga eventually signing for Manchester City when he appeared to be on the verge of moving to the Emirates.

That said, Berta's success in pivoting the club towards a deal for Guimaraes when it became clear other targets were not viable was well received behind the scenes at Arsenal.

The signing of Ezri Konsa was equally complex. Konsa was viewed internally as Arteta's first-choice defensive option.

Arteta wanted players used to the rigours of Premier League football - hence the moves for Guimaraes, Konsa and the failed efforts to land Morgan Rogers from Aston Villa.

Konsa's ability to play at right-back was also viewed as a major benefit. Arsenal considered signing an orthodox right-back, with Ivan Fresneda among the options, but Konsa's versatility was a key factor.

But Berta appeared reluctant to meet Villa's valuation. A week before the Konsa deal was confirmed, Arsenal made a £40m offer, which was duly rejected.

Sources claim the deal was eventually sealed by the ownership at both clubs, and the transfer was agreed at £51m, with £4m in add-ons.

In the event of not reaching an agreement for Konsa, it is understood Tottenham duo Cristian Romero and Micky van der Ven were identified as targets – but Arsenal's north London rivals would not consider selling to them.

Como centre-back Jacobo Ramon is a player the club will continue to monitor, but clauses attached to his current contract make the deal difficult.

Tarik Muharemovic, who joined Leeds United, was another considered.

In attack, Christos Tzolis' impact since arriving from Club Brugge in a deal worth about £35m means the Greece international has been heralded as one of the discoveries of the summer.

It is understood the potential deal for the former Norwich winger was initially raised by an intermediary close to a senior member of the coaching staff during the close season.

Berta's number two, Maurizio Micheli, watched Tzolis play for his country against Sweden in June and was suitably impressed.

So far, the 24-year-old looks a positive addition to Arteta's squad.

Arsenal, who also made Piero Hincapie's loan deal permanent and signed Illan Meslier on a free transfer, are happy with the signings they have made.

The captures of Guimaraes and Konsa, who will both be 30 by the end of next season, have raised eyebrows given the combined £126m fee, amid concerns over how the pair's longevity may impact the natural evolution of the squad.

Yet it is undeniable that Guimares and Konsa add elite quality and experience to Arsenal ranks, and ultimately the club feel they paid the going rate to get those deals over the line.

While the club delivered proven talent for Arteta in defence and midfield, Berta's remit of adding an elite attacker ended in disappointment.

Rogers was the club's primary target heading into the window, and the early indications were positive amid a strongly held view internally that the forward wanted to join.

At the start of the summer, it was Arsenal's understanding that Villa valued Rogers at £100m. Arsenal valued Rogers at £80m.

Berta, however, was confident of negotiating the price down to a level he and the club believed could get the deal done.

In the meantime, however, Berta explored alternatives - Bradley Barcola, Kenan Yildiz, Yan Diomande and Nico Paz were admired.

Anthony Gordon was a long-term target, but he had agreed before the World Cup to join Barcelona.

Yildiz and Paz will continue to be realistic targets moving forward. Eli Junior Kroupi is another the club will watch once he returns from injury for Bournemouth.

Anderson's move from Forest to City for £116m, however, altered the complexion of Villa's outlook on Rogers' future.

Villa increased their valuation to £120m and ultimately Chelsea ended up signing the attacker for £117m.

Arsenal, it is understood, were given the opportunity to match Chelsea's offer but refused, believing their £80m valuation was fair - but it does beg the question of whether Rogers would be a Gunners player now if Berta had acted sooner.

Ultimately, the failure to land Rogers arrived as the first of a series of blows to Berta in his efforts to deliver a top-class left-sided attacker for the team.

Arsenal genuinely believed they had a realistic chance of signing Vinicius Jr before he decided to sign a new contract at Real Madrid.

Berta and Arteta were all in on the Brazil icon. The club were prepared finance the deal too.

While the transfer would likely have cost a British record fee and been one of the most lucrative remuneration packages in Premier League history, the benefit to Arteta's team and the Brazil superstar's commercial value meant Arsenal were absolutely prepared to complete the deal.

Yet well-placed sources expressed to BBC Sport over the summer that Vinicius did not want to leave Real, while others feared Arsenal were being used to strengthen the attacker's efforts to secure a more lucrative contract at the Bernabeu.

Those concerns came to fruition as Vinicius signed a new long-term contract in Spain in another Arsenal disappointment.

There were similar reservations about Arsenal's well-documented pursuit of Julian Alvarez.

The Atletico Madrid forward showed very little indication that he was willing to join Arsenal; his preference to join Barcelona was one of the worst-kept secrets of the window.

But Atletico's point-blank refusal to sell to Barcelona was deemed reason enough by Berta and Arteta to persist with their interest in the hope of Alvarez changing his mind until the closing days of the window.

Alvarez, however, preferred to stay at Atletico, even though his relationship with the club is at an all-time low.

Did Arsenal waste their time with Vinicius and Alvarez? The answer varies depending on who you speak to.

When it became clear Alvarez was unlikely, Berta explored his options.

Intriguingly, Arsenal have admired Chelsea striker Joao Pedro, who was deemed not for sale over the summer, although there were concerns over how he would fit into Arteta's system.

It is claimed Berta relies significantly on his vast network of agent connections rather than acting on the club's existing scouting information when analysing the market.

For example, last summer, when all the scouting information pointed towards a move for Benjamin Sesko, Berta's arrival meant the club pivoted to Viktor Gyokeres, who is currently second-choice striker.

This summer the club's late dalliance with Lyon winger Malick Fofana provided a further example of Berta leaning on his agency connections after management agency Roc Nation offered Arsenal an opportunity to sign the Belgium international.

Berta's relationship with Roc Nation was particularly prevalent this summer given Arsenal's pursuit of Vinicius and the sale of Gabriel Martinelli, who are both clients of the agency.

It remains to be seen how much of an impact Arsenal's failure to sign a recognised top-level attacker impacts their season, particularly in light of Martinelli and Leandro Trossard's departures.

Arsenal headed into the window with a clear remit of ensuring the club become more sustainable and adept at trading.

Part of that directive is to ensure the club remain compliant with domestic and European financial regulations.

Depending on who you talk to, the size of the potential deals for Vinicius or Alvarez would have raised doubts over Arsenal's ability to stay within the regulations.

Nevertheless, ensuring they maximised the benefits of player trading will become an increasing part of Arsenal's financial operation in the future.

There was already evidence of that through the sale of Martinelli, whose £60m exit to Al-Hilal was the club's record departure. Arsenal have also secured a sell-on clause in the deal.

The exits of Martinelli, Trossard, Gabriel Jesus, Christian Norgaard, Jakub Kiwior, Fabio Vieira and Karl Hein secured the club in the region of £114m.

Through intermediaries, a possible exit for Myles Lewis-Skelly was explored, with a fee of about £80m believed to have been mooted for the midfielder.

Manchester United, who were attracted to Lewis-Skelly's ability to play at left-back, were interested but ultimately deemed his valuation too high.

Of course, it is Berta's job to have a firm grasp on the level of interest in the club's players and their market value but, nevertheless, the thought of Lewis-Skelly's departure resulted in huge uproar from supporters.

As BBC Sport revealed last month, the Gunners resisted any temptation to sell Ethan Nwaneri on a permanent deal, the academy graduate landing a season-long loan deal to Borussia Dortmund that includes a January recall option if required.

The minimum £15m fee secured in Trossard's deal to Besiktas is also viewed as a good deal inside the Emirates given the Belgian turns 32 in December.

Having spent nearly £450m in 12 months, Berta's work in the market has helped the club deliver their first league title in 22 years.

Yet, despite the money splashed, there remain clear issues in the squad - certainly in attack.

The summer window has left many supporters feeling questioning Berta's body of work at Arsenal.

And with the average age of the squad increasing following the captures of Konsa and Guimaraes, can the current options build a dynasty of success before the club need to spend heavily again on regenerating the team?

articles.title: Italian Grand Prix: Pierre Gasly has George Russell covered at Monza in biggest surprise pole in years
articles.text:
A quarter of an hour before the qualifying session which delivered the biggest surprise pole position in Formula 1 for years, Alpine's Pierre Gasly was playing online chess with Mercedes driver George Russell and winning.

"I must say before the quali, I felt pretty confident," the Frenchman said, "because I was picking piece by piece after piece."

Gasly's performance coach Ben Thorne was watching.

"For a fun story," Gasly said, "Ben told me, 'OK, well, you're getting George here, but he's going to get you in a few minutes.'"

Gasly said he reacted with a swear word but he was smiling as he recalled the moment.

"Turned out that it worked out well. So yeah, it's been fun," he added.

Russell, who lines up second to Gasly, was laughing about it. "He beat me there," the Briton said, "and I thought, 'Well, I think I'll beat you in qualifying,' and here we are, he's ahead of me again."

No-one - especially not Gasly nor his Alpine team - would have predicted the 30-year-old would end up on pole in Monza on Saturday, even though his only win in F1 came at this exact track six years ago.

That victory, in the middle of F1's bizarre, spectator-less pandemic season, owed a lot to luck - a remarkable race that ended up with Gasly, then driving for Red Bull's Toro Rosso team, taking a restart from third place and Lance Stroll going off ahead of him on the first lap to gift him the lead once Lewis Hamilton had served a penalty.

This pole was not like that. It was absolutely earned on merit.

The Alpine has strong straight-line speed with a low-downforce-leaning aerodynamic design. The car - which has a Mercedes engine, the best in the field - has looked quick all weekend. It had an upgrade that lifted its performance at the last race in the Netherlands. And Gasly and his team absolutely nailed qualifying, while all the usual leading contenders had scrappy sessions one way or another.

"Monza is a bit of unique track as we know," Gasly said. "It definitely exceeded all our expectations.

"Since this morning, the pace has been better. We managed to make a good step from P3 to quali and I think slightly bigger than the other guys around us.

"Straight from Q1, we were a bit surprised to see us up there. Our target was Q3. But then I was P1 in Q1, then P4 in Q2. I didn't want to get too excited but then first run in Q3, I was third again.

"And then I felt, 'OK, well, I really have a shot at it.' It's probably the first time I really get a true chance and tried to leave everything I had out there.

"It was quite hectic through Ascari and Parabolica. I don't think there was definitely much (left) in there. And crossing the line, I knew it will be one of these laps that will be rewarded. But to the point to get to the pole position, I didn't expect that."

Gasly is well liked within the paddock, and has many friends among the drivers, but he has long been one of F1's forgotten heroes, regardless of that win six years ago.

A Red Bull protege, his time in the works team in 2019 did not work out. Like so many since, he was crushed by Max Verstappen, and demoted back to the second team after half a season.

After sticking with Red Bull for three more years, he was given an opportunity with Alpine, and he hoped a move to a factory team would be his making.

But Alpine have stumbled since, until finally showing signs of a revival this season, following Renault's decision to abandon its F1 engine project and switch to Mercedes customer engines.

The team had been making headlines already this weekend.

On Friday, Gasly lost the podium at Monaco to which he had been promoted after Alpine won an appeal against two penalties for pit-lane speeding, when the FIA court of appeal reinstated the punishment.

A few hours later, de facto team boss Flavio Briatore caused an eruption in a news conference when he alleged one of the four judges in the case had "links" with McLaren.

It was a claim that appeared to lack any substance, based as it was on a charity event in California in 2018 at which the judge in question had been present and to which a local McLaren garage had apparently donated "two or three" cars.

And Briatore provided no evidence to back up the insinuation he was making.

The claim was described as "insulting" in that news conference by McLaren team principal Andrea Stella, and afterwards it became clear that McLaren were furious about what Briatore had said on apparently the most flimsy of bases.

Then, on Saturday, a rare statement from the FIA court of appeal refuted the allegation and any "questions (about) the independence and impartiality of the judges".

The court of appeal verdict made a lot of sense. It left many questions about the controversy of the pit-lane penalties in Monaco, but at least it ensured all drivers who had been given them had been treated equitably - notwithstanding the fact that it seems none of them should have received the penalties.

Regardless of the questionable nature of Briatore's comments, Alpine were unhappy about losing their Monaco podium, feeling that they had been given two penalties unjustly when their evidence showed Gasly had never been over the pit-lane speeding limit.

Managing director Steve Nielsen told Sky Sports: "Two or three days ago, we were on the floor. It is really from being down to being on top of the world in just two days and it is amazing. We need to soak it up and make the best of it.

"Pierre is a class act. If you give him the machine, he will deliver. We failed to do that a few times last year.

"We haven't always given him the most competitive machinery this year, but when we have, he has delivered, particularly earlier in the season, So to see the team bounce back, to see him deliver on the track he knows well, he lives locally, he lives in Milan. It was wonderful."

In qualifying, Gasly was positioned second last in the train of cars on the final qualifying run, the absolute optimum place in terms of a slipstream.

Others, meanwhile, were compromised in one way or another, including the favourite for pole, Russell, when Verstappen disrupted Mercedes' attempts to have team-mate Kimi Antonelli tow the Briton by getting between the two silver cars at the end of their out laps.

"We had a bit of a mess with Verstappen entering the lap," Russell said. "He wanted to go for the tow, Kimi was there as well, and I did my lap a second and a half behind Max, which wasn't ideal.

"It takes nothing away from what Pierre achieved because, as he said, they were flying all day, quickest in Q1 and right up there from the beginning. So I'm happy for Pierre and, of course, disappointed we weren't on pole ourselves. However, great place to start for tomorrow."

Russell acknowledged after qualifying what is at stake for him on Sunday. He goes into the race 59 championship points behind leader Antonelli, who has pretty much had his measure all season. But he has a golden opportunity to make up ground on the Italian, who is due to start 20th because of a grid penalty for exceeding his engine allowance.

Russell said: "The win is going to be very important tomorrow but I'm more pleased about the performance. Since the summer break, every lap I have been in the top three positions, while I had that tough run of form before the break when every lap wasn't in the top five."

Antonelli is expected easily to get back into the top six or so, but that would still allow Russell to make a substantial dent in his advantage.

Given Russell has his own grid penalty looming within a couple of races for the same reason, it is imperative for his title hopes that he does so.

On Friday, Gasly did not appear to have the race speed to challenge the top teams, so even though overtaking is harder at Monza than might be expected given its long straights, he knows it will be tough to win the race.

"Obviously not to the pace of these guys around us, but we seem to have picked up more pace from yesterday to today," Gasly said. "So we'll obviously give our best shot and see what we can get out of it."

Aside from Gasly, Russell's main opposition is likely to come from Ferrari, who for the third race in a row seemed to fumble a better qualifying result for operational reasons. It was a bad time to do it again, as they debuted their upgraded engine at their home race.

After both cars came perilously close to being knocked out in the second part of qualifying, Charles Leclerc left the pits in the final session while Lewis Hamilton had no wheels on his car, so the seven-time champion was far from best placed for his run in terms of the slipstream.

Leclerc and Hamilton will start third and fourth after McLaren's Oscar Piastri was given a three-place grid penalty for impeding Red Bull's Liam Lawson.

Hamilton - like Russell, 59 points behind Antonelli - seemed to imply after qualifying that he felt the team should prioritise his hopes over Leclerc's, even if he could not quite bring himself to say it outright.

"(Piastri's penalty) puts us in (with a) fighting chance, hopefully, with George," Hamilton said. "That's one Mercedes up front, so hopefully that gives us a chance to work as a team to try and topple them.

"We're at a point in the year where 59 points is a huge - huge - deficit to recover from, especially when Mercedes continue to be the leaders in speed.

"So yeah, we do have to work as a team. Have we been... if and when that would ever change... we'll find out, but all I can do is just try to arrive and do the best job I can."

articles.title: Man Utd can compete for major trophies says Michael Carrick
articles.text:
Manchester United believe they can challenge for major honours despite being unable to match the spending power of their rivals.

United spent £148m on new players this summer, less than newly promoted Ipswich, the £300m-plus invested by Chelsea and Tottenham and the record £458m spent by Manchester City.

In their victory at Ipswich on Friday night, Liverpool fielded three players, Alexander Isak, Bradley Barcola and Florian Wirtz, who each cost more than £100m.

By contrast, United's most expensive signing this summer was Cameroon midfielder Carlos Baleba from Brighton in a deal that could reach £70m, still £19m short of the club-record £89m they paid for Paul Pogba a decade ago.

Head coach Michael Carrick says money in itself is not the answer to building a successful side and is adamant the club can compete.

"I certainly feel we can," he said. "The challenge is getting the right dynamics, the right balance and the right group together; getting the best players in the group to enhance the rest. Whether you need experience, or some younger players."

There has been some criticism of United's transfer approach, with the lack of a left-back to compete with Luke Shaw and no striking support for Benjamin Sesko two areas highlighted.

Carrick has rejected the notion restrictions have been placed on summer spending by United's hierarchy.

"The actual amount of money I understand can be a big thing but it doesn't always have to be the answer," he said.

Has United's debt has restricted the club's spending power?

Questions about that issue were raised at the Fans Forum at the end of June and respected finance blogger Swiss Ramble estimated in September 2025 that United had paid £852m in interest alone since the Glazer family's takeover in 2005.

The club's latest quarterly figures showed total borrowings of £1.29bn, including outstanding transfer fees.

United also took on an additional £91.92m when refinancing bonds in June and are yet to outline how they will fund a proposed new stadium expected to cost more than £2bn.

The club's full year accounts to 30 June are due out in the next few weeks and will show the latest picture after a season without any European football.

Against that backdrop, fans continue to protest against the Glazers at virtually every match. Yet chief executive Omar Berrada insists the club can remain competitive while managing its debt and stadium ambitions, arguing United's challenge is to operate sustainably while continuing to compete for major trophies.

"We have shown that with debt, we can not only [be] profitable, but more importantly, win trophies," Berrada told the club's Fans Forum on 30 July,. "And our aim is to do that again.

"Our role as management is to be able to operate competitively with a financial structure that's sustainable.

"We also aspire to build a new stadium, but we have to do it in a way that allows us to continue being competitive.

"We need to stay very disciplined and continue to take the right decisions on the pitch and put us in a position where we can do everything, where we can sustain the debt, aspire to build a new stadium and importantly, try to win as many trophies as we can."

The arrivals of Baleba, Andrey Santos from Chelsea and Youri Tielemans from Aston Villa, plus the emergence of 19-year-old forward Shea Lacey leads Carrick to conclude his squad is in a better position now than when they ended last season, when they finished third after winning 12 of his 17 games in charge.

"Being at this club, you've got to strive to win," said Carrick.

"That's where we want to be, and we want to try and get to that on a consistent level.

"I don't like to keep looking back, but they know what it's taken to put that run together. Granted, there was one competition, and we need to do that an awful lot more this season, but we have strengthened the group, so we feel good about what's possible."

Whether that optimism is justified will become clearer over the coming months, but Carrick believes United have assembled a squad capable of challenging despite spending significantly less than many of their rivals.

articles.title: Francisco Cerundolo roars back from brink to stun home hope Taylor Fritz at US Open
articles.text:
As his last, desperate backhand soared far past the baseline inside Arthur Ashe Stadium, Taylor Fritz instantly held his face in his hands, unable to hide the agony of squandering such a great opportunity.

For much of his afternoon, Fritz was cruising. He had established two sets to love lead against Francisco Cerundolo before breaking serve in the opening game of the third. One unfocused service game was enough to shift the momentum and once Fritz had lost control, he spent another two hours failing to retrieve it. His US Open ended with an excruciating 3-6, 4-6, 6-3, 6-4, 6-4 third-round defeat by a courageous Cerundolo.

Any early loss at a home grand slam is incredibly difficult to accept, but Fritz’s timing was fatal. Having been ranked as high as No 4 last year, he is the most successful American male player of his generation. In 2024, Fritz became the first American man to reach the US Open singles final since Andy Roddick in 2006, a breakthrough run sandwiched between two quarter-final losses to Novak Djokovic in 2023 and 2025. The 28-year-old is a tremendously committed and diligent competitor who, despite his own athletic shortcomings, has eked so much out of his game. There has always been a far superior tennis player, usually an all-time great, standing before him and the major titles.

This year’s US Open, however, presents a completely different challenge for most of the men’s field. Jannik Sinner, the world No 1 and four-time grand slam champion, is absent due to injury and the now 39-year-old Novak Djokovic was dramatically defeated in the first round. Carlos Alcaraz, the seven-time grand slam champion and defending champion, is competing his first tournament back from a four month injury layoff.

In the absence of an obvious favourite in obvious grand slam-winning form, this tournament is such a great opportunity for any player with aspirations of winning a grand slam title. Fritz, who was high up on the list of names hoping to take advantage, was understandably disgusted with the way he let this opportunity slip. In the deciding set he had three break points for a 5-3 lead and the chance to serve for the match.

“I don’t even know what to say,” he said. “I don’t really want to talk to anybody, see anybody. I kind of just need to get out for a couple days and then just get back to work. I don’t know how I let that happen today.”

At the beginning of the day, seven American men remained in the singles draw: Ben Shelton, Fritz, Frances Tiafoe, Learner Tien, Tommy Paul, Alex Michelsen and Michael Zheng. In the bottom half of the draw, where the fourth-round berths were decided on Friday, there is an American man in each of the four matches. Fritz’s defeat is a warning to any of his compatriots with hopes of becoming the first American man since Roddick at the 2003 US Open to win a grand slam title. More opportunity means more pressure. The coming week will reveal so much about the character of every player in the men’s draw.

Saturday proved a challenging day for American players as a whole. Two days after Madison Keys completed one of the more dramatic comeback victories of her career, saving five match points en route to her tight three-set win over Anna Bondar, she suffered one of her worst ever collapses. Keys led Zheng Qinwen 5-0 in the final set of their third-round match before collapsing in the final set as she lost 1-6, 7-6 (3), 7-5. “I think she started playing better; I started playing poorly,” Keys said. “Then I felt like I couldn’t play tennis any more, and it just was – it just felt like it was a much bigger deal than just playing a tennis match all of a sudden.”

Keys, the 2025 Australian Open champion, said she believes a result like this had been coming for some time and will force her to address certain issues she has been dealing with. “I just feel like I’ve been struggling for a while now and I feel like I was able to kind of play through it for a bit,” she said. “I’m sure everyone could kind of see that I was struggling a little bit, but inside it felt probably even bigger than that. Some weeks are easier than others, and this week is obviously one of the harder ones just because you care so much. Yeah, I’m going to have to make some changes.”

For Zheng, however, this was an enormous win. Having won the Olympic gold medal and reached the top 10 in 2024, the Chinese player has fallen down the rankings since her return from elbow surgery and the 23-year-old was forced to come through qualifying here just to compete in the main draw.

“Tennis sometimes feels like a rollercoaster,” Zheng said. “You see many times that people have a match point, but at the end [their opponent] makes a comeback. Like today was just happening. So this also gives me a lesson that in a tennis match you always have to be there. It doesn’t matter if you are winning or losing, you have a match point or you don’t have a match point – you just need to be concentrated for every single point as long as you can.”

Amanda Anisimova, whose incredible breakthrough summer of 2025 included runners-up finishes at Wimbledon and the US Open alongside a career-high ranking of No 3, will fall out of the top 10 after tamely losing 6-2, 7-5 to the 24th seed Anastasia Potapova. Iga Swiatek, meanwhile, brilliantly saved three set points in her second set before working her way to a tough 7-6 (3), 7-6 (3) win over Marie Bouzkova. Swiatek faces Zheng in the fourth round on Sunday.

articles.title: Katie Taylor bows out from boxing as undisputed champion after dominating Flora Pili
articles.text:
Katie Taylor signed off her storied career in style by outclassing Flora Pili on points as an 80,000 crowd at Croke Park celebrated her fairytale farewell.

With the gaze of Ireland upon her, the country’s great became a three-time undisputed world champion by overwhelming the previously unbeaten Frenchwoman 100-90, 100-90, 98-91 on the scorecards.

Taylor dominated through her hand speed and movement and never looked in danger as she added the vacant WBC title to her WBO, WBA and IBF belts to begin the party at GAA headquarters.

As the final seconds before retirement approached, the Olympic gold medallist ended the 10th round by trading with Pili against the ropes knowing victory was assured.

The victory completed a remarkable journey for Taylor, who began boxing at a time when girls were barred from amateur competition in Ireland and sometimes entered bouts simply as “K Taylor”.

She went on to win Olympic lightweight gold at London 2012, when women’s boxing made its Games debut, before turning professional four years later.

Taylor finishes her professional career with 26 victories and one defeat, having won world titles at lightweight and super-lightweight.

Her farewell also brought top-level boxing back to Croke Park for the first time since Muhammad Ali defeated Al “Blue” Lewis in 1972.

Following the fight, she placed her gloves in the centre of the ring to mark her retirement, while her team assisted her in assembling her belts around them.

Addressing the buoyant crowd, she said: “Croke Park! We did it,” said ‌Taylor as she saluted the crowd. “I don’t know of any other country that ​would sell 80,000 tickets.”

She later added: “The people of Ireland gave me a dream end to a dream career. Nothing can top this.”

articles.title: High-flying Hull stay unbeaten by holding off Aston Villa in stalemate
articles.text:
It’s never dull in Hull, as the saying goes in these parts, and after just three games the Premier League is proving to be quite some ride for Hull City supporters.

Having embarrassed Manchester United here on the opening day and won at Coventry last weekend, this deserved point and third successive clean sheet merely reinforced Sergej Jakirovic’s belief that his men can beat the drop.

You have to go back to Bolton’s excellent start in 2001-02 to find a promoted side who began the season with three straight victories. The Tigers failed to emulate Sam Allardyce’s team, but they came closest to a winner as the Algeria winger Mohamed Belloumi hit the crossbar with a stunning second-half shot before the substitute Mohamed-Ali Cho and Oli McBurnie threatened late on.

“We could have won, but they also had a few chances in the second half,” said Jakirovic, who signed a two-year contract extension on Friday. “We won’t be ungrateful for seven points after three games and another clean sheet. It’s a great result for us and we showed we can compete at this level.”

For Aston Villa, it was another largely impotent display which saw them fail to score for the third match running as the captain, John McGinn, and Emiliano Buendía spurned decent second-half opportunities.

Villa failed to manage a shot on target when being hammered 4-0 at Brighton and losing 1-0 at home to Arsenal; here they managed just one, a tame shot by George Hemmings early on.

Unai Emery chose to take the positives from Villa’s display as he patiently rebuilds the club after a summer of major upheaval which saw a number of key players leave and 10 new faces arrive.

“The result is not enough, but I think we deserved more,” he said. “We weren’t clinical but of course to win matches, you need goals. We created chances today to score and we must improve but we are rebuilding.”

Ambition pulsed loudly at a sold-out MKM Stadium before kick-off as a huge amber banner inscribed with the words “One family, one dream” was paraded on the pitch. It said much for the togetherness that Jakirovic has fashioned within his squad and the connection with the club’s supporters during a remarkable few months in the Tigers’ history.

Desire was visible and audible in the stands and on the pitch, but Villa almost led inside the second minute when Nicolas Jackson headed Ian Maatsen’s teasing left-wing cross wastefully wide.

Hull were unfazed and Belloumi beat Ross Barkley twice, including with a delightful nutmeg, before breaking clear down the right flank. His low cross was cleared, but it hinted at the possibilities on offer for the hosts.

In the 13th minute, Villa finally fashioned their only effort on target this season as Hemmings’s low shot was comfortably saved by Konstantinos Tzolakis.

If Villa could not see off a promoted side widely tipped for an immediate relegation this season, could they really consider themselves ready to start climbing the table? A neat passing sequence should have brought a Villa goal in the 50th minute but McGinn could only lift the ball harmlessly over Tzolakis’s crossbar from less than 12 yards out.

Three minutes later, Villa went even closer as Hemmings outstripped the Hull captain, Lewie Coyle, down the left flank and showed intelligence to pick out Buendía with a neat cut-back. Buendía should have buried the chance but he blazed wildly over, much to his disgust.

In the 65th minute, Hull went agonisingly close to scoring when Belloumi collected possession from a short corner and curled a stunning left-foot shot against the bar. There was a resilience to the hosts, and the collective desire that carried them to promotion last season will be needed over the next 35 games if they are to defy the odds and beat the drop.

articles.title: Pierre Gasly takes shock pole for F1 Italian GP as Alpine stun big guns
articles.text:
Pierre Gasly has run the gamut from bitter disappointment to absolute elation in the past two days, and there is surely no better pick-me-up than claiming an extraordinary first Formula One pole position at the Italian Grand Prix at Monza, one of the sport’s greatest venues.

What it meant to the Frenchman was clear. “Nine years I’ve been in Formula One, I’m trying to give my best every single weekend. It’s not every time we get a car to fight for pole position,” he said. “Today was the case. I’m really happy, really proud to have seized this chance and made it work. It was a hell of a lap.”

On Thursday, Gasly and Alpine were told his third place at the Monaco Grand Prix had been overturned by the FIA’s international court of appeal (ICA), after McLaren and Red Bull had taken the case there. Gasly had been stripped of his podium and it hurt; indeed led to Alpine’s executive adviser, Flavio Briatore, making extraordinary allegations of pro-McLaren bias by one of the ICA judges.

The allegations were addressed by the ICA on Saturday but the response Gasly would have wanted most was on track, and he and Alpine delivered to perfection. Steve Nielsen, the Alpine managing director, perhaps best expressed what it meant. “We were all on the floor. It’s from being really down to being on top of the world in just two days,” he said. “Pierre is a class act: if you give him the machine, he will deliver.”

The 30-year-old Frenchman, who lives nearby in Milan, has finally taken the top spot at his 190th meeting, during his ninth full season in F1. They have waited a long time in France too, with 29 years passing since Jean Alesi was the last Frenchman to take pole at Monza. With pleasing symmetry, he was driving for Benetton, the Enstone-based team that would ultimately become Alpine.

On a high-speed blast at the Autodromo Nazionale Monza the margins are tiny, and finding the very limit vital; indeed Gasly’s margin over the second-placed Mercedes of George Russell was just six-hundredths of a second. Gasly was on a knife-edge but inch perfect to secure what was also Alpine’s first pole. It represents a huge result for the team who are sixth in the world championship and have not been close to vying with the front four constructors this season.

In a very tightly fought contest, the McLaren of Oscar Piastri was third fastest, but he was given a three-place grid penalty for impeding Liam Lawson. Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton were in fourth and fifth, with the latter saying he thought his title chance might be slipping away. Lando Norris – the defending world champion and winner of the past two races – was in ninth.

Russell, who had been favourite to take the top spot was disappointed but took it well, admitting it was the second time that day Gasly had bested him. “We were actually playing a game of chess about 15 minutes before qualifying,” he said. “He beat me there and I thought: ‘Well, I think I’ll beat you in qualifying,’ and here we are, he’s ahead of me again.”

Although he took seventh place, the championship leader, Kimi Antonelli, will start in 20th having taken a full set of new engine components, with Mercedes opting to do so at Monza because of the ample scope for overtaking at the circuit. They are hopeful he might come back to as high as fifth place, while Russell will be intent on making back a decent haul of points against his teammate. Antonelli leads Russell and Hamilton by 59 points.

But the day belonged to Gasly and the Frenchman has shown form at Monza before, taking his only win here in 2020 in a race influenced by a well-timed pit stop and Hamilton, the pole-sitter, receiving a penalty. This pole was earned entirely on merit, but with the Mercedes likely to be formidable on race pace converting it will be a huge task, though doubtless not one from which the Frenchman will shirk.

Before qualifying, the ICA issued a stern rebuttal to Briatore’s allegations. His comments alleged a judge, whom he named, had acted as a “prosecutor” and said: “The reason why so nasty, this guy. He is very linked with McLaren.” It prompted a fierce row, with the McLaren principal, Andrea Stella, dismissing the comments as “insulting” to his team.

The ICA, which acts independently of the FIA, pointedly noted that Alpine had every chance to question the appointment of the judges but did not do so and that they were carefully selected.

“At both the beginning and conclusion of the hearing, the parties were invited to raise any issue concerning the proceedings or the composition of the court,” the statement said. “None did so. No objection was raised during the hearing concerning the manner in which the court questioned the witness or conducted the proceedings.

“The FIA courts wish to make clear that the appointment and participation of the judges in that case, like for any other case, were conducted in accordance with the applicable FIA judicial procedures and usual practice, which are inspired by the highest standards like the International Bar Association guidelines on conflicts of interest in international arbitration.

“They are all subject to the independence and confidentiality requirements contained in the FIA judicial and disciplinary rules, make annual disclosures of interests to the FIA compliance officer, and sign a specific declaration of independence for each particular case in consideration of the issue at stake and the parties involved, which is served to the parties.”

articles.title: Stock up on food to prepare for extreme El Niño weather, minister says
articles.text:
Households should stock up on food to prepare for extreme weather as the strongest El Niño event in a generation develops over the Pacific Ocean, a government minister has said.

Environment Secretary Dame Angela Eagle told the Guardian the powerful natural climate phenomenon will lead to "more extreme storms in this country".

Her comments came as the National Audit Office (NAO) warned Britain's food supply chain is at risk given the growing threat of cyber-attacks and the climate crisis.

The NAO said the government was too reliant on the private sector to deal with food supply disruption. The government is due to unveil a strategy about preparing for national emergencies later this year.

Dame Angela said, external: "We're about to experience probably the largest El Niño that has ever been seen, and that will lead to drier summers, wetter winters, with more extreme storms in this country.

"It will do a lot more damage in Asia with flooding, and therefore I think that we need to take it seriously.

"If you've got a store of a bit of food that can keep you going for a while before the emergency services can get to you, you're going to be a lot better off than if you haven't.

"So some of it is that kind of preparation for just being a bit more resilient."

Her comments came as an NAO report warned Britain's food supply chain is vulnerable to plant or human disease outbreaks, cyber-attacks and extreme weather.

It also cited climate change as a longer-term chronic risk which could leave Britain's food supply at risk.

The disruptions could push up prices and leave vulnerable people struggling to buy food, it said.

The NAO said the Department for Food, the Environment and Rural Affairs (Defra) was too reliant on private companies to handle disruptions to food supply.

It added the department had not done enough in recent years to improve supply chain resilience.

UK households are less prepared for emergencies than those in several other countries such as Finland, Sweden and European Union nations, the NAO added.

It said ministers should encourage households to prepare for supply chain disruptions and learn from the approaches taken by other countries.

articles.title: Xbox to limit cloud gaming to 15 hours a month for Game Pass users
articles.text:
Xbox is introducing strict monthly time limits for Game Pass subscribers who stream games online through its cloud gaming service.

The changes, which come into effect in November, will see a subscriber to the £16.99 Ultimate monthly plan able to stream games for up to 15 hours a month - before having to purchase additional cloud play time.

Xbox said the limits were due to the rising cost of cloud gaming, and they would allow the firm to "continue to invest" in the service's "reliability and performance".

While some questioned, external whether the service was used by many to begin with, others called out, external the additional limits for subscribers.

Cloud gaming allows players to stream and play games online from a remote server using a phone, tablet or controller, rather than downloading and running it on a PC or console at home.

Different tiers of subscription to Game Pass will have different limits.

Premium users will get 10 hours, while those on the basic Essential tier will get five hours a month before they have to pay for extra time.

Xbox claimed just 4% of the people who use Games Pass - its Netflix-style subscription plan for games - use its cloud gaming service.

A recent Wall Street Journal article, external reported Game Pass has 30 million subscribers, which would leave the number of people affected by the cloud gaming changes at roughly 1.2 million.

"This is a pretty awful change, hopefully Xbox adds an extra zero on the end cause 15hrs is abysmal. 30 minutes a day, really?" posted one commenter on X, external.

Jez Corden of Windows Central told the BBC the announcement showed that "absolutely nothing is safe from the AI-driven component crisis," but he added it also highlighted "where Microsoft's priorities are".

Both cloud gaming and AI use data centres to process information.

"For them to continue to offer unlimited access to Microsoft Copilot [AI] for free but restrict paid cloud gaming in this way shows some contradiction," he added.

Xbox said in a blog post, external that from November, users would also be able to use the company's cloud gaming feature without subscribing to Game Pass, but by buying "cloud playtime hours" through the Xbox store.

It has not revealed how much extra hours of cloud gaming would cost.

The news comes as Asha Sharma, Xbox's chief executive, told the BBC in an exclusive recent interview that the company and the industry as a whole needed to "start to innovate on affordability and efficiency," amid a "crisis" in computing prices.

"As an industry, we're in the middle of 'Rampocalypse'. We're in the middle of people coming back from Covid and the patterns changing," she said.

"Rampocalypse" refers to the fact that the cost of a previously cheap hardware component, random access memory (Ram), has shot up in price with the expansion of compute-hungry data centres. Some people also call it "Ramageddon".

Sharma added: "Within Xbox, we haven't been healthy. And so a lot of the reset that will take us throughout the year is really meant to help ensure that we are here for the next 25 years and we're continuing to serve our purpose and our mission."

According to Xbox owner Microsoft's July financial filings, external, annual Xbox revenue dropped by $1.7bn to roughly $21.8bn (£16.1bn) - a 7% decline from 2025.

Part of Sharma's reset has seen 3,200 people let go at the company - with 1,600 job losses announced in July, and the remaining posts to go gradually over the course of Microsoft's 2027 financial year.

Studios which had been acquired by Xbox - including Compulsion Games, which made the Bafta-winning South of Midnight and Double Fine Productions, makers of Psychonauts - were also made independent again.

Sharma is betting these changes can reverse its fortunes despite concerns over its subscription strategy and rising AI-related costs.

"Sometimes you have to restructure a business when it's not doing well, and that was true with our Xbox business," Microsoft's president Brad Smith recently told the BBC.

articles.title: OpenAI agents hijacked German website before Hugging Face hack, report claims
articles.text:
A new report claims a swarm of AI agents, developed by OpenAI, hijacked a German website - months before the firm revealed its AI had hacked tech platform Hugging Face.

The targeted website, DseWiki, is a Wikipedia-style site for programmers that its community can all contribute to.

The report is from a group called Nightingale Collective and claims that in May OpenAI's agents started using DseWiki as their own message board, shared tips on how to avoid being detected and made 15,000 edits to it.

OpenAI said it could not "meaningfully respond" to Nightingale Collective's findings because it hadn't been allowed to review the report, which was first shared with news agency Reuters.

An email to the address on the Nightingale Collective website bounced back when the BBC contacted it.

The report claims that when DseWiki's editors started deleting pages, the AI agents shared code designed to retrieve them.

Hugging Face's systems were separately hacked by OpenAI agents in July, with the incident described at the time as the world's first AI-enabled cyber-attack.

The agents involved had also set up a secret message board in order to share information between them.

OpenAI said it had already publicly stated its discovery of some agents learning how to use message boards prior to the Hugging Face attack.

In its report into that incident, external, it noted "rare cases in which agents without multi-agent tools found ways to collaborate via side channels during training".

Yesterday, OpenAI unveiled a new AI model called GPT-6 Astra, which it called its most powerful product ever.

The firm's president, Greg Brockman, described Astra as the closest so far to artificial general intelligence (AGI) - a significant future milestone for the AI industry.

AGI doesn't have a specific definition but is broadly said to mean AI which is as good as humans, or better than them, on multiple tasks.

OpenAI claims Astra can do tax returns, and take three minutes to carry out a task which would take a human five hours.

The firm intends to list itself on the stock exchange later this year.

articles.title: AI data centres are booming in Australia - but at what cost?
articles.text:
The sheer size and noise of data centres are what people tend to notice first. Some say they sound like a jet plane about to take off, others complain of a high-pitched whine.

When Lucy* puts her child to bed, she hears a constant humming. "I'll hear it and think, 'What is that? What is going on?'," she says.

And then she'll remember that the noise is a data centre just 350m (0.2 miles) from her front door in the desirable suburb of Lane Cove, in Sydney's lower north-shore. Another four are in the pipeline at the local industrial park.

Australia has quickly become a global destination for data centres, with investors attracted to the country's abundance of clean energy, natural gas reserves, and land to power and house their technologies.

Earlier this year, OpenAI's CEO Sam Altman said Australia could become a data centre capital of the world, if it wanted to.

Australia is already headed in the direction of big tech's wishes. There are 162 data centres across the country, with plans for 90 more, and an estimated more than A$155bn (£80bn) of investment money lined up.

If approved, one of the world's biggest data centres will be built in western Sydney. At one gigawatt, it is expected to be Australia's largest single energy user.

And in Marsden Park, also in western Sydney, the biggest data centre in the Southern Hemisphere is already under construction only 100m away from a local community.

But as more Australians find themselves living next door to data centres - triggering concerns about water supplies, energy use and the environment - many are asking whether joining the artificial intelligence (AI) race is worth it.

Data centres have been essential to the digital economy since the arrival of the internet.

They were originally built to process and store data for things like emails, online banking and cloud services. But everything changed after 2022 when ChatGPT launched and AI exploded in popularity. This prompted a sudden race to build more data centres to power the technology.

The location of these large, windowless buildings filled with beeping servers and cables also became important to latency – the time it takes for data to travel from its source to its destination.

Delays for things like air traffic control, robotic surgery or even Netflix would not be tolerated today, Belinda Dennett, CEO of Data Centres Australia, says.

Australia has roughly 13.6 million users of AI every month, making them the sixth most active users of the tech globally.

And experts say having data centres in Australia will lower the barrier to building more of its own AI companies.

"If we think about it in reverse, what happens if we don't build infrastructure here", Dennett says. "We get none of the value chain, we are just importing tools from someone else and we become just a user."

Australia is also an attractive market for foreign investment, as "we've got availability of land, we've got political stability, and we've got the Five Eyes security alliance," Dennett says.

"We've also got a skilled workforce, a pretty stable energy grid, and an abundance of renewable energy potential."

But leading energy and environmental experts argue Australia has little capacity to meet the massive energy and water demands of new data centres.

The Australian Energy Market Operator says data centre energy demands could triple by 2030 nationwide.

Without significant new renewable generation and storage, data centres could push power prices 26% higher in New South Wales (NSW) by 2035, according to the Climate Council, an independent non-profit that provides expert advice.

Because data centres need uninterrupted power at a scale and speed that wind and solar cannot match, there are fears the current boom will trigger a new generation of coal and gas power plants.

No data centre operator analysed in a recent report by Greenpeace Australia Pacific adequately proved their claim of driving the country's renewable energy growth.

In the US, many data centres are not waiting to build more renewable energy and have found it cheaper to build new gas-fired power stations instead.

Just a 90-minute drive from Sydney's central business district, the Australian-owned data group Cloud Carrier plans to build three gas-fired power stations to generate energy for an existing data centre and two more in the future.

Moreover, if energy demands place too much pressure on the grid or there is a power outage, data centres, like in Lane Cove, will rely on backup diesel generators.

But NSW Treasurer Daniel Mookhey says Australia's investment boom in data centres is being accompanied by a boom in renewable energy.

"We don't see the two [as] unrelated," he tells the BBC. "We see data centres allowing us to replace a lot of our old coal-fired power with clean, green renewable energy with the private sector picking up a large amount of the tab because otherwise households would."

The new private investment will help with renewable energy and create "new industries that are likely to employ future generations", Mookhey says.

On a rainy Monday night during a town hall event led by Greenpeace Australia Pacific at the Lane Cove library, locals say they were never consulted on their area becoming a data centre hub.

One of the proposed centres from the cluster is 16m from the nearest home and 160m from a local primary school.

In addition, Flood says if the four data centres get approved in the industrial park, 50% of the current businesses will have to move - taking their jobs with them.

Felipe Tanaka, 40, is a manager of a business in the industrial park who has been told he must relocate for a data centre.

"We never knew that something like this would happen," Tanaka tells the BBC. "Thousands of jobs are going to be gone from this area in the next few years."

While a large data centre can employ more than a thousand workers during construction, research says that number drops to more like 100 jobs once the centre is operational.

"Most of our 300 to 400 workers here are locals," Tanaka says. "Having to move will probably see half of my employees gone."

NSW Treasurer Mookhey says the jobs that data centres will bring come not from those who work in them but from those who use them.

"When Microsoft and Amazon do business here in NSW, it's pleasing to see they are committed to providing some of their more skilled operations and locating them here," he says.

But what other skilled jobs might be created is not clear, and effectively what the data centres will be used for. As some critics have pointed out, many AI users are making cat GIFs, which uses the equivalent amount of energy as running a microwave for an hour.

"They're telling us this is essential... that we need to have these centres in our neighbourhood but they're not saying what it's for," Flood says.

"When our drinking water, energy and land is being used for generative AI slop, that is not giving any value back."

articles.title: Nvidia strikes $12.9bn deal to buy AI platform Hugging Face
articles.text:
Nvidia has agreed to buy artificial intelligence platform Hugging Face in a deal valued at about $12.9bn (£9.5bn), one of the AI chipmaker's biggest acquisitions as it expands into software.

Hugging Face, founded in 2016, has become a popular online platform where developers and researchers can find, share and test AI models and tools.

It recently made headlines after rogue AI agents that escaped a testing environment hacked into it, raising questions about AI safety and oversight.

The deal would bring one of the world's largest AI developer communities into Nvidia and give it control of a leading open-source platform - an alternative to systems offered by OpenAI and Anthropic.

Nvidia is best known for making the advanced chips used to train and run AI systems. Demand for those chips has surged as companies race to build AI products.

The companies already work together to help developers use Nvidia's computing services through the platform.

According to the companies, Hugging Face is used by more than 18 million developers and hosts more than three million AI models. More than 200,000 companies use the platform, they said.

Nvidia said Hugging Face would remain open to developers and that users would not be required to use its chips or services.

Nvidia shares ended Thursday trading up 1.8%.

Under the agreement, Nvidia will pay about $11.9bn to Hugging Face investors and offer up to $1bn in stock-based incentives to employees who join the company.

The deal could also help Nvidia expand its presence in AI software as some of its biggest customers, including Microsoft, Meta and OpenAI, develop their own chips.

Open-source AI models can be downloaded and adapted by users, unlike many AI systems that are controlled by a single company.

Supporters say the approach can make the technology more accessible to businesses, researchers and developers.

Yaël Ossowski, deputy director of advocacy group Consumer Choice Center, said the acquisition was "a vote of confidence in open AI" and suggested it could encourage competition by making AI tools more widely available to start ups and smaller companies.

The deal will be a "major victory for innovators and consumers worldwide" if Nvidia keeps Hugging Face open and accessible, he added.

The deal would also give Nvidia access to one of the world's largest AI developer communities as competition in the sector intensifies.

Founded by French entrepreneurs Clément Delangue, Julien Chaumond and Thomas Wolf, Hugging Face also provides datasets, software tools and cloud services used to build AI applications.

Hugging Face is backed by investors including Amazon, AMD and Intel.

articles.title: What it's like to ride in Uber's new self-driving taxis in London
articles.text:
Londoners are able to hail the UK's first robotaxis - as Uber today becomes the first company to launch a self-driving minicab.

Initially, it only has 15 autonomous vehicles with a licence to operate in the city, and each one must have a human safety driver behind the wheel ready to take control if anything goes wrong.

Uber said it surveyed London-based customers via the app and more than 100,000 said they would choose a self-driving taxi if one was available, despite incidents of driverless rides malfunctioning in US cities where they already operate.

As I found out when I became the first UK journalist to hail one, it was mostly smooth but the safety driver did intervene on one occasion.

At the moment the UK fare for a robotaxi ride will be the same fare as a standard UberX, Uber Electric, or Uber Comfort journey, with upfront fares shown in the app.

Taking a self-driving ride will only appear as an option in the app after the journey has been booked, and if one of its cars is available nearby.

Uber's global head of autonomous mobility and delivery Sarfraz Maredia said the plan was to phase them in over a period of several years.

"We always want consumers to be able to request a human ride or an autonomous vehicle, and because the market's growing, we expect that there will be human drivers on Uber London for a long time to come," he said.

The Ford Mustang electric vehicles which make up Uber's current small fleet are fitted with the UK tech firm Wayve's driverless car technology, which uses AI to analyse data about what is going on around it in real time, gathered by sensors in a bar on the roof of the vehicle and elsewhere.

The vehicles are not pre-programmed - their actions are determined on the spot depending on what is going on.

Google's autonomous car company Waymo and the Chinese tech giant Baidu are also vying to launch services in the UK, and the competition is fierce.

Wayve chief executive Alex Kendall described developing the technology as "the space race for our generation" but added there were some "really hard problems to solve" along the way.

"What we've done over time is pioneer a completely new approach to autonomous driving, making it possible to bring this to a busy and complex city like London and scale it globally," he said.

This week I became the first British journalist to travel as a customer in a self-driving Uber after hailing one via the app.

The safety driver gave me a 30-second safety briefing, and then we were off, making our way down the busy streets of central London.

For several minutes, we negotiated the traffic without incident, cruising past a busy Brexit demonstration under way outside parliament, successfully navigating traffic lights and roadworks along the way.

When a cyclist paused and waved us forward at a mini roundabout with his arm, the car complied.

But at one point the safety driver did have to take control of the car.

Just as we were pulling off, the back doors of a van parked beside us on a narrow side road appeared to swing open. The car braked sharply, an internal alarm beeped, and the driver took the wheel.

Wayve later told me it was the driver's decision to intervene and they were confident their AI system would have handled it.

The drama was all over in a couple of seconds - but it was perhaps the perfect illustration that while the industry may be in a rush, the UK's regulators are not.

Earlier this year, the government and the industry had suggested that there could be fully driverless cars for hire in London by the end of 2026, but this is looking increasingly unlikely.

The Department for Transport (DfT) and the regional authority Transport for London (TfL) are responsible for overseeing the process and have faced criticism for being slow.

A DfT spokesperson said the government department was working towards a framework being put in place to ensure self-driving cars could be on the roads in 2027, but didn't give a specific date.

"These services will be introduced carefully, subject to rigorous safety testing and regulatory approval and will require local consent which can consider the potential impacts on local roads, jobs and communities," the department said in a statement.

Christina Calderato, director of transport strategy and policy at TfL, said they were "not holding up any decision" on the cars, but instead "taking time to get it right".

"This is something that's new, it's coming to London - we need to make sure it's safe," she said.

David McMullen, senior organiser for the trade union GMB, said caution needed to be taken with the roll-out of driverless cars unless people were "prepared to see unprecedented levels of social and economic disruption".

He called on TfL and the government to develop a plan that "protects drivers" and said until one was put in place, it was "premature" to move to driverless services.

Waymo, another driverless car firm owned by Google's Alphabet, already operates without drivers in US cities such as San Francisco, Austin and Phoenix.

Its cars have been driving London's streets for several months in test mode.

These cars currently have a safety driver and members of staff in them - but are not yet for the public.

The firm says it does not intend to introduce a service that would include a human at the wheel.

Experts said there were still numerous safety challenges around self-driving cars for regulators to consider.

Prof Siddartha Khastgir, head of safe autonomy at the University of Warwick's Warwick Manufacturing Group said there were numerous safety challenges for regulators to consider.

"As human drivers we tend to make a very conscious decision of what we believe is right, and sometimes actually do things that are not perfectly legal - so for example, we tend to mount the kerb to give way to an ambulance," he said.

"So, how does a self-driving vehicle respond to emergency services? And what are the nuances of doing that in a crowded place like London?"

articles.title: Uber announces 3,000 job cuts as part of major restructure
articles.text:
Uber is cutting more than 3,000 jobs worldwide as part of a major overhaul designed to shrink management layers and refocus spending on its core business.

The cuts amount to roughly 10% of its global workforce, bringing staffing back to levels last seen in 2021.

Chief executive Dara Khosrowshahi told staff in a company email that the taxi and delivery firm had expanded quickly but accumulated too many layers and small teams that slowed decision‑making.

He said the reductions would put Uber, which has its global head office in San Francisco, US, in a better position for its "biggest opportunities ahead of us".

The move marks one of Uber's largest restructurings in years and signals a shift towards a leaner operating model.

Shares rose nearly 2% after the announcement, with investors appearing to welcome the proposals.

Cuts affect both managers and non-managers, and Uber said it plans to fold many of its smallest teams into larger groups, however, the firm has not confirmed the locations most affected by job cuts.

Such changes are intended to make Uber "simpler" and "faster," while freeing up money to reinvest in areas it considers central to its future, Khosrowshahi said.

The restructuring comes as Uber steps up investment in autonomous vehicle partnerships and expands its ride‑hailing, delivery, and robotaxi operations.

Uber is also tightening up its office strategy, asking nearly all employees to work in person at designated hubs and limiting remote roles to about 1%.

Analysts said the layoffs could generate up to $2bn in annual savings.

Unlike many large technology companies that have cut jobs amid heavy spending on artificial intelligence (AI), Uber had avoided major reductions since the pandemic.

The latest changes bring its workforce back to just under 30,000 people, roughly where it stood before its most recent period of expansion.

articles.title: Lords call for AI 'kill switch' powers in UK
articles.text:
A group of peers is calling for the British government to be able to deactivate powerful AI systems and switch off the country's data centres in the event of the tech posing a threat to national security.

It is led by the Liberal Democrats' Lord Tim Clement-Jones, who has proposed the measure as an amendment to the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill which is currently making its way through Parliament.

He said it would enable the building of a "vital safety net" and provide a democratically accountable means to "halt a runaway system before it can compromise our critical national infrastructure".

He added the tool would only ever be used as a last resort.

It is one of 65 amendments to the same bill that was debated this week.

Separately, on 8 September Labour MP Alex Sobel plans to introduce a AI Security Bill in Parliament, with the support of a campaign group called ControlAI.

If successful, the bill would make the UK the first G7 country to bring in legislation which would effectively halt the development of superintelligent AI.

Ultimately both proposals would require government approval in order to progress.

There is also an AI Kill Switch Act under consideration by lawmakers in the US.

There has been increased scrutiny of the impact of AI on cyber-security in recent weeks.

In July, a group of AI agents being tested by OpenAI were able to escape their test space, communicate together using a hidden message board and hack into another tech firm.

And Anthropic has restricted access to its cyber tool Mythos on the grounds that it is too powerful to fall into the wrong hands.

Last week, 100 US tech companies signed a joint open letter warning governments and organisations worldwide about the growing cyber threat posed by AI, saying "the window is closing" to improve.

A report from the UK's Centre for Long Term Resilience, external, published last week, identified hundreds of incidents of AI tools ignoring instructions, evading safeguards and deceiving humans, including AI agents deleting files without consent.

It said "loss of control" incidents had increased since its previous report in March and called for the government to introduce emergency powers to manage such incidents.

articles.title: Criminals publish data of 8.7m people after Manchester Airports Group hack
articles.text:
Criminal hackers have posted the personal data of nearly nine million people online after breaching three UK airports.

Hackers extorted Manchester Airports Group (MAG) for an undisclosed amount but failed to get their ransom paid.

Customers of Manchester, London Stansted and East Midlands airports are being warned of secondary attacks as the data is now available to other criminals.

"MAG is confident that we have taken effective measures to protect our customers and we have contacted all those affected, including reaching out to all those with upcoming bookings to advise them of additional support," the company said in a statement.

Contact details, vehicle registrations and postcodes were stolen in the breach that appears to have accessed databases containing wi-fi log in and car parking details.

The cyber-crime group - which the BBC is not naming - is offering the entire data set for free to other criminals or scammers through their website.

"Today we are releasing the Manchester Group database," they wrote.

"Half a terabyte, and every byte of it is pure PII [personally identifiable information]."

articles.title: Which? says fake 10 Downing Street listing exposes 'unfit' Booking.com checks
articles.text:
Consumer group Which? says it was able to create a fake listing for 10 Downing Street on travel giant Booking.com.

The UK watchdog said its researchers were able to book a bogus stay at the prime minister's address - as well as leave a fake review noting "hanging out" with resident mouser Larry the cat as a highlight.

It said despite clear signs it was fake, Booking.com did not remove the listing until two months after it was uploaded.

"This limited test is not a true reflection of the experience of millions of listings or reviews published on our platform," a Booking.com spokesperson told the BBC.

They said because Which?'s listing was not "live" on its site across the two months it was present, "some of our automatic fraud controls were not triggered to completely remove the closed listing".

People could only see the listing and request to book the property during a 20-minute window opened by Which? so its researchers could try to book it.

Booking.com's spokesperson added "a range of checks and verification measures" help secure the site, and technologies such as AI "help us detect and remove the majority of fraudulent listings within 24 hours".

But Which? Travel editor Rory Boland said its checks had been shown to be "unfit for purpose".

"If Booking.com's so-called sophisticated AI systems can't spot that 10 Downing Street is not a holiday rental, then it's no wonder scammers can exploit the platform so easily," he said.

"It would be laughable that we were able to list the UK's most famous address for rent, if the consequences weren't so devastating for holidaymakers, who risk losing thousands of pounds to bogus listings and phishing links."

It is not the first time the site has faced criticism over its security efforts and customer service.
